entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Muʿīn al-Dīn Sulaymān Parwāna, commonly known as Pervâne, was a pivotal Persian statesman whose career, spanning the mid-13th century, profoundly shaped the political landscape of Anatolia during a period of intense geopolitical upheaval. As the de facto ruler of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rûm from the 1260s until his execution in 1277, Pervâne navigated the treacherous currents between the fragmenting Seljuk authority, the dominant Mongol Ilkhanate, and the expansionist Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt. His cunning diplomacy and pragmatic alliances, often shifting, were instrumental in maintaining a semblance of order and continuity in a region reeling from the Mongol conquests, even as they ultimately led to his downfall.

Rising through the Seljuk bureaucracy, Pervâne consolidated power after the Battle of Kösedağ in 1243, which had rendered the Seljuks vassals of the Mongols. He strategically married the widow of Sultan Ghiyāth al-Dīn Kaykhusraw II, strengthening his claim to influence. He masterminded the appointment and deposition of several puppet Seljuk sultans, including Kaykaus II and Kilij Arslan IV, ensuring his control over the administration and treasury. His most daring political maneuver was inviting the Mamluk Sultan Baybars into Anatolia in 1277, hoping to dislodge the Mongols, a gamble that backfired spectacularly following Baybars's swift withdrawal after the Battle of Elbistan.

His actions directly influenced the power balance between the Ilkhanate and Mamluks in the Near East.

entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Muʿīn al-Dīn Sulaymān Parwāna, known simply as Pervâne, was a pivotal Persian statesman whose Machiavellian political maneuvering dominated Anatolian affairs in the latter half of the 13th century. As the de facto ruler of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rûm, he navigated the treacherous geopolitical landscape between the fragmenting Seljuk authority, the ascendant Mongol Ilkhanate, and the formidable Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt. His career epitomized the complex power struggles and diplomatic exigencies faced by regional potentates caught between larger imperial forces, profoundly influencing the trajectory of Anatolia from a centralized sultanate to a mosaic of independent emirates.

Rising through the Seljuk bureaucracy, Pervâne shrewdly consolidated power, becoming the most influential figure in the Sultanate after the devastating Mongol victory at the Battle of Kösedağ in 1243. He effectively governed Seljuk Anatolia for nearly three decades, from 1256 until his death in 1277, often holding the title of vizier and controlling the succession of puppet sultans. His strategic acumen was demonstrated through his administrative reforms, the construction of numerous caravanserais and mosques, and his adept, albeit ultimately doomed, attempts to play the Ilkhanids against the Mamluks. A notable episode was his brief, desperate alliance with the Mamluk Sultan Baybars I, inviting him to Anatolia in 1277, which resulted in Baybars' victory over the Mongols at Elbistan but ultimately triggered a brutal Mongol reprisal against Seljuk lands.
